prompt: How do large decompilation projects or tools speed up mass compile-and-diff loops for mwcc: running mwcceppc natively or under wibo/wine with lower per-invocation cost, compile result caches, objdiff CLI in batch or as a library, parallel/distributed permuter farms, incremental ninja builds? Give repo URLs, licences and any measured invocation cost or throughput. For every claim give the primary source (repo file, issue, PR, compiler manual) and state it as a falsifiable prediction: 'with X, mwcc emits Y; with X', it emits Y''. Mark anything unverified.

query: What per-invocation time and throughput do decompilation projects actually measure when they run the old Metrowerks compiler many thousands of times, and where do they publish those numbers?

How long does a single Metrowerks compiler invocation actually take on native Windows, under Wine, under wibo and under Linux wrappers when a GameCube or Wii decompilation project builds a file, and who measured it on what hardware?

Why does process startup and filesystem translation make the same Windows compiler binary run so differently across Wine, a lightweight loader and native Windows, and how much of a permuter's time goes to compiling versus scoring the resulting object against the target?

Why does launching a 32-bit Windows compiler under a compatibility layer cost so much per call, and which parts of that cost (process startup, loader, file system, licence checks, temporary files) can be removed without changing the generated machine code?

What measured timings have people published for launching an old 32-bit Windows compiler thousands of times in a row, and how much of each launch goes to starting the process versus actually compiling the code?

What happens to the correctness of cached or incrementally rebuilt compile results when compiler version, flags, include files, pragmas or environment differ slightly, and when have projects seen a speedup produce object files that differ from the original toolchain or a wrong match?

Why does a compile that looks identical to a previous one sometimes get treated as the same when it is not, for example when compiler version, flags, header contents, embedded paths, timestamps or environment settings differ?

Which projects ignored the elaborate speedup machinery and still reached high match rates with plain sequential builds or a single machine, and what about their codebase or workflow made that sufficient?

What do decompilation contributors report about how much time and compute they actually spent on automated permutation of a function before a human rewrite of the code got it to match, and who measured it?

What happens to the final few percent of a game rebuild when the original compiler's output depends on build order, hidden state, or merged identical code, and how do teams recognise that a function can never match?

learning: [DERIVED][LOW] When file-heavy tools run across a translation boundary (Linux tools reading Windows drives through WSL2), the slowdown comes from the boundary, not the tool, and ranges from roughly 2x to 10x or worse. Moving the project onto the native filesystem changes performance more than configuration tuning, so a compile-heavy loop like a permuter's would likely gain more from file placement than from faster machines. — Capacidad: You can stop attributing slow, file-heavy build or compile workloads to the compute layer itself and instead decide where the work's files live before buying hardware or blaming the tooling. — Evidencia: S8 gives a 2x-10x slowdown range for filesystem translation in WSL2 and says location matters more than tuning; applying that to compiler/permuter loops is my inference, not stated. — Ledger: C4 (S8)

[DERIVED][LOW] Wine startup passes through the host dynamic loader, a Unix-side ntdll, creation of Windows process structures, connection to a separate server process, and mapping of a Windows-side ntdll before the program runs. Each compile launched by an automated search loop pays this setup, so per-invocation overhead, not just compile speed, plausibly explains Wine's gap versus native Windows. — Capacidad: You can treat a Windows program under Wine as a multi-stage startup (host loader, Unix-side library, server process, Windows-style environment) and so expect fixed per-launch overhead that matters most when a tool is launched thousands of times. — Evidencia: S7 traces the startup stages in detail but gives no timings; the link to repeated-launch cost in a permuter is inferred. — Ledger: C5 (S7)

[DERIVED][MEDIUM] The Modern Warfare 2 rebuild jumped from an error-ridden ~80% (fabricated or deleted logic, needing a dedicated reviewer agent) to 83% byte-exact once correctness was judged by byte-for-byte comparison with the original compiler. That made the review agent unnecessary and let cheap models (Haiku, Luna) carry the work, cutting cost substantially. What made a simple setup sufficient was the codebase having a checkable answer key, not extra machinery. — Capacidad: You can stop buying more compute or elaborate parallel tooling for AI-driven rebuild projects and instead invest in a mechanical pass/fail check against the original, which is what made cheap, single-pipeline work sufficient. — Evidencia: MW2: 83% of all functions byte-matched, 99% had source, 600-700 billion tokens (about 300 billion on the cheap Luna model), after the verifier replaced AI review; figures are self-reported by the developer. — Ledger: C18 (S32)

[DERIVED][MEDIUM] On Snowboard Kids (2,145 functions, 100% in about 83 days), roughly 4.8% of matching commits (about 41) involved expert intervention. The developer estimates that without experts on the IDO compiler, matching would have stalled around 89-90%. Snowboard Kids 2 stalled twice (25% to 58%, then ~75%) and needed community members for its last 10 functions, taking 596 days overall. — Capacidad: You can plan for a plateau near 89-90% on automated, easiest-first work and budget for specialist humans and community help for the last stretch, rather than expecting more automation to finish it. — Evidencia: Specific figures: 4.8% expert commits (~41), 89-90% estimated plateau, 83 vs 596 days; the 4.8% and the plateau are the developer's own rough estimates, not measured values. — Ledger: C19 (S32)

[DERIVED][LOW] In the Modern Warfare 2 rebuild, the leftover functions would not match byte for byte however often they were revised, because of nondeterministic compiler behavior and an inability to reproduce the linker step that merges identical functions into one. The developer stopped at 83% of all functions matched, with source existing for 99%, judging that further matching would only consume tokens without real improvement, after spending an estimated 600 to 700 billion tokens. — Capacidad: You can declare a rebuild project finished at a high-but-not-perfect match rate once the remaining items are shown to be structurally unmatchable, instead of continuing to fund effort that only burns tokens. — Evidencia: Single self-reported source gives 83% matched, 99% with source, and 600-700 billion tokens, with the code unpublished and unverifiable by third parties. — Ledger: C24 (S32)

[DERIVED][LOW] On Snowboard Kids, roughly 4.8% of matching commits (about 41) involved experts familiar with the original SGI IDO compiler, and the lead estimates the match rate might have plateaued around 89 to 90% without them. Easiest-first automated processing stalls, as seen when Snowboard Kids 2 jumped from about 25% to 58%, rose to about 75%, then stalled again and needed community help on its last 10 functions. — Capacidad: You can budget for the last stretch as a scarce-expertise problem, planning for specialist knowledge of the original toolchain rather than assuming more automated effort will close it. — Evidencia: Stated figures: 4.8% of commits (about 41), 89-90% plateau estimate (an estimate, not measured), and 25%/58%/75% stall pattern; both S32 and S40 repeat the 4.8% and 89-90% numbers. — Ledger: C25 (S40)

[DERIVED][LOW] Three different units circulate: matched bytes of total code (Melee, 100%), matched functions of all functions (MW2, 83%), and functions with any source regardless of match (MW2, 99%). The Halo project shows 99.5% in one README versus 23.25% on a public tracker, so a headline number can mean a verification mode, a different metric, or a stale fork rather than progress. — Capacidad: You can treat any quoted completion percentage as unusable until its denominator and verifier are stated, and stop comparing figures across projects. — Evidencia: S32 documents the differing denominators and the Halo 99.5% vs 23.25% conflict; S38 independently explains the 99.5% is an optional verification build, not completion (tracker shows 7.17%). — Ledger: C26 (S32, S38)
